title: Operation Queen
pull: Thousands of planes, then the infantry

facts.text: On 16 November 1944 the Allied air forces flew Operation Queen, which the US Army's official history calls the largest air attack of World War II in direct support of ground troops.
The plan called for more than 4,500 planes, about half of them heavy bombers. Fog over the bases in England and on the Continent kept many on the ground that morning.

About 1,200 Eighth Air Force heavy bombers (1,191 in the US Army history, 1,204 in other counts) dropped 4,120 tons of fragmentation bombs around Eschweiler, Weisweiler and Langerwehe. Fragmentation bombs were chosen to hit troops without cratering the roads the Americans would need.

RAF Bomber Command struck the towns of Duren, Julich and Heinsberg behind the front to block German reinforcements. The US Army history counts 1,188 RAF heavy bombers and 5,640 tons, almost half of it on Duren; other counts of the RAF force are lower.

Remembering the bombs that fell short on American troops in Normandy, planners kept the bomb line two miles in front of the troops. One American soldier, in a 3d Armored Division artillery unit, was killed by stray bombs.

The guns joined in. On the First Army front 694 guns fired an hour long preparation of about 45,000 light, almost 4,000 medium and 2,600 heavy shells, helped by tank guns, mortars and a battalion of 4.5 inch rocket launchers. With the Ninth Army's 552 guns, 1,246 artillery pieces took part.
At 12:45 the infantry of the US First and Ninth Armies attacked along the line from near Geilenkirchen to the Hurtgen Forest, heading for the Roer River.

The bombing disappointed. Most forward German positions survived, and prisoners from one German division put their losses at 1 to 3 percent. But telephone lines were cut. "I tried to use the telephone," one German said, "but the line had been cut by the bombardment."

Bad luck struck the German 47th Volks Grenadier Division, which was arriving by train in the Roer towns as the bombs fell. An artillery battalion caught at the Julich railroad station was all but wiped out.

The 1st Infantry Division's 16th Infantry fought through the woods toward the village of Hamich under heavy shelling. By 17 November its 1st Battalion's rifle companies, which had started with about 160 men each, were down to 60 or 70 men, one to 100.

On 18 November the 16th Infantry cleared Hamich house by house, and Hill 232 above it fell after fifteen artillery battalions fired on it at once. That night a German lieutenant leading a counterattack lost his way in the dark and drove straight into Hamich, where American artillery broke up his column.

declassified.fact: To stop bombers hitting their own troops, the Americans laid out a whole system of markers: two giant white panels behind the lines, a row of eleven captive balloons borrowed from the British flying at about 2,000 feet, and bright panels near the front. Sixty four 90 mm antiaircraft guns fired red flak bursts to show the bombers exactly where the American front line was.

film.shot_notes: Signal Corps reel, silent, 6 min 21 s. 00:00 to 01:10: 104th Division infantry NE of Stolberg, 8 Nov 1944 (not used). NOON: LIB 662, T27 multiple rocket launchers of the 18th Field Artillery, VII Corps, at Mausbach, 16 Nov 1944, 01:16 to 02:56: crews behind the launcher frames, loading 4.5 inch rockets, launchers firing and smoke rolling over the field (best firing 02:20 to 02:52). Open on a firing or loading shot. 7 P.M. SECOND CUT: Hamich, Germany, 20 Nov 1944 (slate 02:56 and 06:08, cameraman Laurence), 03:00 to 06:04: 1st Division infantry file through the ruined village in the rain, jeeps and trucks on muddy streets, a soldier close up at 03:52; open on infantry walking past burning houses at about 04:16. No shot of the noon stretch appears in it.
